Question 1
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of decreasing x where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 116xm/s2. If P has a displacement of 0m when its velocity is −2m/s, find v in terms of x.

a
v(x)=−14x2+64
b
v(x)=−12x2+16
c
v(x)=1464−x2
d
v(x)=−x2+4
e
v(x)=1216−x2
Submit

decision.explanation: Using a=v dv/dx gives v dv/dx=x/16. Integrating, v²=x²/16+C. Since v=-2 at x=0, C=4. Motion is in the direction of decreasing x, so v is negative: v(x)=-√(x²+64)/4.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $0\,m$ when its velocity is $-2\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059489/assets/ba6a85da04d9ba03bcdba9b938dac208a770933310cd25c19bf0ec3e19ef17c7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (\frac{1}{16}x)\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=-2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}(0)^{2}+C \\ 2 & =0+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+4 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}({x}^{2}+64) \\ v & =\pm \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.
$$

Question 1

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of decreasing x where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 116xm/s2. If P has a displacement of 0m when its velocity is −2m/s, find v in terms of x.

a
v(x)=−14x2+64
b
v(x)=−12x2+16
c
v(x)=1464−x2
d
v(x)=−x2+4
e
v(x)=1216−x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is 116xm/s2, we have

dvdt=116x.

Using the fact that dvdt=ddx(12v2), we can rewrite our equation as ddx(12v2)=116x.

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have ∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫(116x)dx which gives the general solution 12v2=132x2+C.

Now, since x=0m when v=−2m/s, we can find the value of the constant C, as follows: 12v2=132x2+C12(−2)2=132(0)2+C2=0+CC=2

Therefore, 12v2=132x2+2v2=116x2+4v2=116(x2+64)v=±14x2+64.

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing x, we have that v(x)<0, so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore, v(x)=−14x2+64.

content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $0\,m$ when its velocity is $-2\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059489/assets/ba6a85da04d9ba03bcdba9b938dac208a770933310cd25c19bf0ec3e19ef17c7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (\frac{1}{16}x)\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=-2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}(0)^{2}+C \\ 2 & =0+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+4 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}({x}^{2}+64) \\ v & =\pm \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059489/assets/4e0b8b816ca3b86fa90ea785df1308f53a4763baa2c2aa2192b9d7bfa0259855.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(4{x}^{3}+4x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4{x}^{3}+4x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4{x}^{3}+4x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (4{x}^{3}+4x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & ={1}^{4}+2(1)^{2}+C \\ 3 & =3+C \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2} \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{2({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2})}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=2$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{2({2}^{4}+2(2)^{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{48} \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of increasing x, away from a fixed origin O. When the displacement of P from O is xm, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is (4x3+4x)m/s2. If v=6m/s when x=1m, find the velocity of P when x=2m.

a
5m/s
b
32m/s
c
4m/s
d
26m/s
e
43m/s
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is (4x3+4x)m/s2, we have dvdt=4x3+4x.

Using the fact that dvdt=ddx(12v2) we can rewrite our equation as ddx(12v2)=4x3+4x. Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have ∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫(4x3+4x)dx

which gives the general solution

12v2=x4+2x2+C.

Now, since v=6m/s when x=1m, we can find the value of the constant C, as follows: 12(6)2=14+2(1)2+C3=3+CC=0

Therefore,

12v2=x4+2x2v2=2(x4+2x2)v=±2(x4+2x2).

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing x, we have that v(x)>0, so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore, v=2(x4+2x2).

Finally, the velocity of P at x=2 is given by v=2(24+2(2)2)=48=43m/s.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms the earlier answer: integrating a=v dv/dx gives v²=2x⁴+4x², using v²=6 at x=1. At x=2, v²=48, and increasing x requires v>0, so v=4√3 m/s. The displayed incorrect result applies to the deliberately submitted option a.

decision.explanation: Since x>0 and acceleration points toward O, a=-2/(x²+1). Using a=v dv/dx and integrating gives v²=-4 arctan(x)+C. The condition v²=π at x=1 gives C=2π. Thus at x=3, v=-√(2π-4 arctan(3))≈-1.1345 m/s, which rounds to -1.1 m/s. The negative root follows from motion in decreasing x.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059489/assets/3278eca2ae91f59c7c20d91f9190611291924dcc0cd6ffe74456552ba8400335.png)

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=-\sqrt{\pi }\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(-\sqrt{\pi })^{2} & =-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+C \\ \frac{\pi }{2} & =-2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+C \\ C & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of decreasing x where x>0. When the displacement of P from O is xm, its velocity is vm/s, the magnitude of its acceleration is 2x2+1m/s2 and the acceleration is directed toward O. If v=−πm/s when x=1m, find the velocity of P when x=3m. Round your answer to one decimal place.

a
−1.1m/s
b
−0.9m/s
c
−2.6m/s
d

e

Submit

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle P is 2x2+1m/s2 and is directed toward O, we have dvdt=−2x2+1.

Now, since v=−πm/s when x=1m, we can find the value of the constant C, as follows: 12(−π)2=−2arctan⁡1+Cπ2=−2⋅π4+CC=π

Therefore, 12v2=π−2arctan⁡xv2=2(π−2arctan⁡x)v=±2(π−2arctan⁡x).

Since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing x, we have that v(x)<0, so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore, v=−2(π−2arctan⁡x).

Finally, the velocity of P at x=3 is given by v=−2(π−2arctan⁡3)≈−1.1m/s, rounded to one decimal place.

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=-\sqrt{\pi }\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(-\sqrt{\pi })^{2} & =-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+C \\ \frac{\pi }{2} & =-2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+C \\ C & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x \\ {v}^{2} & =2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v=-\sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =-\sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡3)} \\  & ≈-1.1\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of increasing x. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, its acceleration is 4x+1m/s2. Initially, P is at the origin O and has velocity v=4m/s. Find x as a function of time t.

a
 x(t)=(t+2)4/3
b
 x(t)=(3t+1)4−1
c
 x(t)=(3t+1)4/3−1
d
 x(t)=(4t+1)3−1
e
 x(t)=(t+2)2/3−1
Submit

decision.explanation: Using a=v dv/dx gives v²=16√(x+1)+C. Initially x=0 and v=4, so C=0. Since v>0, dx/dt=4(x+1)^(1/4). Separating and integrating yields (x+1)^(3/4)=3t+1, hence x(t)=(3t+1)^(4/3)-1.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ its acceleration is $\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059489/assets/ee516744d915553bf962b498af522cf0006d42c5d0e0e2a003e6f385dd069e4a.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8\sqrt{x+1}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8\sqrt{x+1}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =8\sqrt{0+1}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8\sqrt{x+1} \\ {v}^{2} & =16\sqrt{x+1} \\ v & =\pm 4\sqrt[4]{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4\sqrt[4]{x+1}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4\sqrt[4]{x+1}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4\sqrt[4]{x+1} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{x+1}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{x+1}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{4}{3}(x+1)^{3/4} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+1)^{3/4} & =3t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{3{C}_{1}}{4}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+1)^{3/4}=3t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{3/4} & =3t+1 \\ x+1 & =(3t+1)^{4/3} \\ x & =(3t+1)^{4/3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of increasing x. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, its acceleration is 4x+1m/s2. Initially, P is at the origin O and has velocity v=4m/s. Find x as a function of time t.

a
 x(t)=(t+2)4/3
b
 x(t)=(3t+1)4−1
c
 x(t)=(3t+1)4/3−1
d
 x(t)=(4t+1)3−1
e
 x(t)=(t+2)2/3−1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is 4x+1m/s2, we have dvdt=4x+1.

Using the fact that

dvdt=ddx(12v2)

we can rewrite our equation as

ddx(12v2)=4x+1.

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have ∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫4x+1dx

which gives the general solution

12v2=8x+1+K.

Now, since x=0m when v=4m/s, we can find the value of the constant K, as follows: 12v2=8x+1+K12(4)2=80+1+K8=8+KK=0

Therefore,

12v2=8x+1v2=16x+1v=±4x+14.

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing x, we have that v(x)>0, so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

v(x)=4x+14.

Now, we know that v=dxdt. Therefore, we have the equation dxdt=4x+14.

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to t, we have

dxdt=4x+141x+14dxdt=4∫1x+14dxdtdt=∫4dt43(x+1)3/4=4t+C1(x+1)3/4=3t+C where C=3C14.

We're given that x=0 when t=0. Therefore, C=1, and the particular solution is

(x+1)3/4=3t+1.

Finally, writing x in terms of t, we have

(x+1)3/4=3t+1x+1=(3t+1)4/3x=(3t+1)4/3−1

Thus it satisfies the acceleration and both initial conditions. The incorrect result shown applies to the deliberately submitted option b.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ its acceleration is $\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059489/assets/ee516744d915553bf962b498af522cf0006d42c5d0e0e2a003e6f385dd069e4a.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8\sqrt{x+1}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8\sqrt{x+1}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =8\sqrt{0+1}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8\sqrt{x+1} \\ {v}^{2} & =16\sqrt{x+1} \\ v & =\pm 4\sqrt[4]{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4\sqrt[4]{x+1}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4\sqrt[4]{x+1}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4\sqrt[4]{x+1} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{x+1}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{x+1}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{4}{3}(x+1)^{3/4} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+1)^{3/4} & =3t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{3{C}_{1}}{4}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+1)^{3/4}=3t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{3/4} & =3t+1 \\ x+1 & =(3t+1)^{4/3} \\ x & =(3t+1)^{4/3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of increasing x where x≥0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, the magnitude of its acceleration is 8e1−xm/s2 and is directed toward O. Initially, P is at x=1m and has velocity v=4m/s. Find x as a function of time t.

a
 x(t)=ln⁡(t+1)+1
b
 x(t)=4ln⁡(2t+1)−1
c
 x(t)=e−2t
d
 x(t)=2e−2t−1
e
x(t)=2ln⁡(2t+1)+1
Submit

decision.explanation: Acceleration toward O is a=-8e^(1-x). Integrating v dv/dx=a gives v²=16e^(1-x)+C. The initial conditions x=1, v=4 give C=0, so dx/dt=4e^((1-x)/2). Integrating with x(0)=1 yields e^((x-1)/2)=2t+1, hence x(t)=2 ln(2t+1)+1.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at $x=1\,m$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059489/assets/f08c9d1e8dce3c0ae7c37719cadc3fc60bf5de3030ce8c44ca7528a98f3abf7e.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -8{e}^{1-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =8{e}^{0}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =16{e}^{1-x} \\ v & =\pm 4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4{e}^{(1-x)/2} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{(1-x)/2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\text{d}x & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=1$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{(x-1)/2}=2t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+1 \\ \frac{x-1}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x-1 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1)+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of increasing x where x≥0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, the magnitude of its acceleration is 8e1−xm/s2 and is directed toward O. Initially, P is at x=1m and has velocity v=4m/s. Find x as a function of time t.

a
 x(t)=ln⁡(t+1)+1
b
 x(t)=4ln⁡(2t+1)−1
c
 x(t)=e−2t
d
 x(t)=2e−2t−1
e
x(t)=2ln⁡(2t+1)+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P has magnitude 8e1−xm/s2 and is directed toward O, we have dvdt=−8e1−x.

Using the fact that

dvdt=ddx(12v2)

we can rewrite our equation as

ddx(12v2)=−8e1−x.

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have ∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫−8e1−xdx

which gives the general solution

12v2=8e1−x+K.

Now, since v=4m/s when x=1m, we can find the value of the constant K, as follows: 12v2=8e1−x+K12(4)2=8e0+K8=8+KK=0

Therefore, 12v2=8e1−xv2=16e1−xv=±4e(1−x)/2.

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing x, we have that v(x)>0, so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

v(x)=4e(1−x)/2.

Now, we know that v=dxdt. Therefore, we have the equation dxdt=4e(1−x)/2.

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to t, we have

dxdt=4e(1−x)/21e(1−x)/2dxdt=4∫e(x−1)/2dxdtdt=∫4dt∫e(x−1)/2dx=∫4dt2e(x−1)/2=4t+C1e(x−1)/2=2t+C where C=C12.

We're given that x=1 when t=0. Therefore, C=1, and the particular solution is

e(x−1)/2=2t+1.

Finally, writing x in terms of t, we have

e(x−1)/2=2t+1x−12=ln⁡(2t+1)x−1=2ln⁡(2t+1)x=2ln⁡(2t+1)+1.

content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at $x=1\,m$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059489/assets/f08c9d1e8dce3c0ae7c37719cadc3fc60bf5de3030ce8c44ca7528a98f3abf7e.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -8{e}^{1-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =8{e}^{0}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =16{e}^{1-x} \\ v & =\pm 4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4{e}^{(1-x)/2} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{(1-x)/2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\text{d}x & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=1$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{(x-1)/2}=2t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+1 \\ \frac{x-1}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x-1 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1)+1.\end{aligned}
$$
